title: Your first week with Claude
for: Anyone who has just opened Claude and does not know what to do next.
intro: Most of this is short. Steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 take fifteen minutes each; step 3 is Anthropic's own 2.5-hour Claude 101, and stopping there still leaves you better off than most people.

steps.title: Claude is not one tool. It's six.
steps.why: Start here because most confusion is not about prompting — it is not knowing that Claude is several different products. Five minutes now saves a week of looking in the wrong place.

steps.title: Get started with Claude
steps.why: Now open the thing itself and do one real task. Reading about it any longer is procrastination.

steps.title: Claude 101
steps.why: By now you have had a generic, disappointing answer. Anthropic's own beginner course is the fix, and at 2.5 hours it is the one step here that is not short — it is the single highest-value stretch of this path, not the single highest-value hour, and the two are different promises.

steps.title: What are Projects?
steps.why: Once you repeat a task twice, you need somewhere to keep the context. Projects is that place. Learning this earlier would have been abstract.

steps.title: Why do AI models hallucinate?
steps.why: Before you trust Claude with anything that matters, understand exactly how it fails. This is the step people skip and later regret.

steps.title: Get started with Claude Cowork (Help Center)
steps.why: Last, because working on your own files only makes sense once you trust the answers. Read it before you point Claude at anything real.

title: Getting good at Claude Code
for: Developers who have installed Claude Code and are getting mediocre results.
intro: The gap between installing Claude Code and being fast with it is configuration and habits, not model quality. The reading is short. The practice is what takes a week.

steps.title: Claude Code 101
steps.why: Anthropic's own course. Do this before reading anyone's tips, so you know which behaviours are the tool and which are the person writing about it.

steps.title: Best practices for Claude Code
steps.why: The best-practices page. Densest thing written about Claude Code, and everything after this assumes you have read it.

steps.title: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
steps.why: Read this third and not later, because it invalidates a lot of 2025-era advice you will otherwise absorb.

steps.title: Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions
steps.why: Now that your setup is right, this is where the speed comes from — knowing which commands quietly destroy your prompt cache mid-session.

steps.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
steps.why: Context engineering is the skill that separates people who get good output from people who get plausible output. It only makes sense once you have felt a long session degrade.

steps.title: A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code
steps.why: Last, because orchestration is worth nothing until single sessions are reliable. Names the failure modes you will have hit by now.

title: Using Claude on work you put your name to
for: Writers and marketers whose byline goes on it, and who would rather not explain themselves later.
intro: The order runs from what job Claude has, through the tells everyone else is trained to spot, to what you owe the reader. The last step is the one people skip and it is the one with consequences.
total_time_label: about an hour and a quarter

steps.title: Claude, Editor
steps.why: First, decide what job it has. This is a writer using Claude as an editor rather than a ghostwriter, and settling that question now is what makes every later step a craft problem instead of an ethics problem.

steps.title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
steps.why: Second, learn the symptoms before trying to treat them. Wikipedia's editors have catalogued what AI prose actually looks like, and you cannot prompt your way out of a tell you cannot name.

steps.title: How to Stop Claude Writing Like an AI
steps.why: Only now is this useful. It is the treatment for the symptoms in step 2 — read in the other order it is a list of fixes for problems you have not learned to see yet.

steps.title: The Ethics of Using AI
steps.why: Last, and last on purpose: everything above makes the work harder to detect, which is exactly why disclosure has to be the step you finish on. Craft is what you owe the page. This is what you owe the reader.

title: Product work without waiting for engineering
for: Product managers who have the question, the users and the context, and keep having to queue for someone else's sprint.
intro: Steps 1 to 4 need nothing but a browser — stop after step 4 and you can already synthesise research, keep it somewhere, delegate the repeatable parts and know what is safe to paste in. Step 5 needs a terminal, and it is fair to decide that is not your job.

steps.title: Claude for Product Managers: Synthesizing User Research
steps.why: Start with the work only you do. Synthesising research is where Claude pays for itself fastest and it needs no setup at all — a chat window and the interviews you already have.

steps.title: Getting started with projects in Claude.ai
steps.why: Second, because one good synthesis is a party trick and a repeatable one is a habit. Projects is where a product area stops being forty loose chats you cannot find again.

steps.title: Claude Cowork for Product Managers: A Working Guide
steps.why: Third: hand over the parts that repeat. This comes after Projects because delegation without somewhere to put the output just moves the mess.

steps.title: Use Claude Cowork safely
steps.why: Fourth, and deliberately not first. Safety guidance is abstract until you know what you would actually delegate — which step 3 just taught you. Read it before the first time you point Cowork at real customer data.

steps.title: Claude Code for PMs: The Beginner's Guide
steps.why: This step needs a terminal, and if that is a no then stop here — the four above stand on their own. It is last because it is the only one that asks you to change how you work rather than what you work on, and because the PM shelf leans heavily on Claude Code; this is the gentlest way in.

title: Using Claude for research without embarrassing yourself
for: Researchers and academics who want the speed without the retraction.
intro: The order matters more here than anywhere else. The failure modes are specific and the consequences are public.

steps.title: Reduce hallucinations
steps.why: Start with the failure, not the feature. Fabricated citations are the one mistake that ends careers, and this is the clearest account of when they happen and how to cut them.

steps.title: What are Projects?
steps.why: Projects is where a literature review actually lives. Set it up before you have forty loose chats.

steps.title: Claude AI and Literature Reviews: An Experiment in Utility and Ethical Use
steps.why: Now read someone who actually tried it and reported what broke, with the guard rails from step 1 in place.

steps.title: Connect and integrate your local Zotero library with Claude Cowork
steps.why: Connect your own library. Until Claude can see your actual sources, everything above is a demo.

steps.title: ICMJE Recommendations — Use of AI in Publishing
steps.why: Before you submit anything, read what the ICMJE expects you to declare. This is not optional and most people learn it too late.

title: Analysing your own data without getting the numbers wrong
for: Analysts with a spreadsheet, a deadline, and somebody who will ask where the number came from.
intro: The arc is your data rather than Claude: get it in front of the model, know what happens to it, then learn the difference between Claude reading your numbers and Claude actually running them. Only the last step needs a terminal, and you can stop before it.

steps.title: Upload files to Claude (Help Center)
steps.why: Nothing below works until your data is in front of Claude, and every other guide in this catalogue assumes you did this already. It is also the only step that tells you what will be refused — the size ceilings differ between a chat and a Project — before you find out the slow way.

steps.title: How long do you store my data?
steps.why: Second, and second on purpose. The writing path puts disclosure last because a writer discloses at publication, after the craft. An analyst decides at upload, before anything: once somebody else's data is pasted, reading the retention terms afterwards changes nothing. Anthropic's own numbers, and narrow ones — consumer plans only, and the page never once says the word attachment.

steps.title: Introducing the analysis tool in Claude.ai
steps.why: Now the idea the rest of the path rests on: Claude can run real code against your file instead of reasoning about the numbers in prose. Here for the concept and not the click-path — it is nearly two years old and the feature has since been renamed to Code execution and file creation, which lives under Settings then Capabilities and can be switched off.

steps.title: How to Use Claude for CSV Data Analysis (The Honest Guide)
steps.why: Fourth, because step 3 is only half of it: Claude has that code-running mode and does not always reach for it. This is where a capability becomes a habit, and it is the step that explains every total that has ever come back confidently wrong.

steps.title: Claude Code for Data Analysis: Excel-Free Answers From CSVs
steps.why: This one needs a terminal, so stop here if that is not your working day — the four steps above stand on their own and an analyst who lives in Excel has already got the whole point. If it is, this is where checking becomes reproducible: rerunnable scripts over silent cell edits, argued from Panko's finding that 94% of spreadsheets already contain errors.

title: Judging AI's design output
for: Designers deciding whether to trust what Claude just handed them — not the rest of the job, just this slice of it.
intro: The arc is judgment, not craft: two honest critiques of what AI prototyping and AI research actually get wrong, the method to test it yourself, one real task to try it on, then the line that ties it together. This covers about a fifth of a designer's job — deciding whether to trust what Claude just produced — and says nothing about the other four fifths.

steps.title: Good from Afar, But Far from Good: AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts
steps.why: Start here because the temptation is to assume a slick AI-generated screen is finished work. NN/g ran the actual comparison — AI against a human designer on the same brief — and the finding holds the whole path together: it hits the brief and misses the craft.

steps.title: AI Can't Replace Real Research in Empathy Mapping
steps.why: Second, because the same trap shows up in research, not just visuals — Claude can cluster notes you actually collected, and it cannot manufacture a user you never spoke to. Read this while step 1's skepticism is still fresh, before you drift back to trusting output by default.

steps.title: Testing AI with Real Design Scenarios: Evaluation Methodology and Prompts
steps.why: Third: now the method, not just the finding. This is deliberately the companion piece to step 1 — six real prompts and the four criteria NN/g judged every output against — and its own skip_if says to read the findings first, which by now you have.

steps.title: Analyze patterns in user feedback (use case)
steps.why: Fourth, on a live task instead of someone else's write-up. Synthesizing real feedback is where the empathy-mapping trap from step 2 shows up in your own inbox — the tension between a real pattern and an echo chamber stops being theoretical here.

steps.title: The UX Researcher's Guide to Claude, Claude Cowork, and Claude Code
steps.why: Last, to widen the lens from one task to daily practice — which Claude surface actually fits which research job — and to end on the sharpest line in this path: statistical coherence is not research validity. A synthesis that smooths over an edge case has failed at the finding level, no matter how confident it reads.
